Physical (or mineral) sunscreen is a sunscreen which works by using small particles of zinc oxide and/or titanium dioxide to block the sun. Chemical sunscreens use chemicals which absorb or scatter the sun.

Physical sunscreens are considered better for the environment because chemical sunscreens wash into oceans and bleach coral reefs. Chemical sunscreens more common and most major brands of sunscreen I've looked at (coppertone, generic store brands, neutrogena, etc.) have chemical sunscreens as the basic type and physical/mineral sunscreens as a more niche product for sensitive skin or hippie types. Physical sunscreens can be worn off more easily than chemical ones, and may leave a white cast or white streaks on your skin. Both varieties of sunscreen have their positives and negatives.

Personally, I prefer mineral sunscreen. There are several varieties of chemical sunscreen that sting my skin and cause it to turn red (including Octocrylene and Oxybenzone), and I'd much rather avoid this completely. Additionally, I am white and I do not tan. Mineral sunscreens often produce a "white cast", or a slight white tint to the skin. (You can also purchase tinted sunscreens if you want a more flesh-toned tint.) This is blurs my skin just enough that I don't really need foundation to look polished.
Physical Sunscreen vs. Chemical Sunscreen: What is your preference?

Ah – the glass question! Well, much like anything out there, the answer is “It depends” because depending on the optic you’re looking at, the glass itself will come from different places. Heck – even sometimes one single optic will have various different lenses made in different parts of the world that all converge together to go into one riflescope, binocular, spotting scope, etc. Most of the world’s glass in its raw form comes from China – and that’s due to the fact that they just have the right resources and minerals to actually make glass more so than any other reason. The most important factor that goes into glass quality is how it is cut, ground, coated, etc and that gets into the second part of your question which is not really something that we can speak to unfortunately as that is proprietary information. What we can tell you, though, is that lens types, curvatures, coatings, etc. are all done specific to each individual optical system and all those things are engineered into the optical system to optimize image quality for the given performance and price point each product is trying to hit. Out of curiosity – is there a particular reason you’d like to know about the origins and makeups of our glass and coatings? Aside from being proprietary, we’ve never really seen the need to market that information simply because glass is just one of so many components to an overall optical system, it really wouldn’t be much help in determining how good or bad any optic is compared to another.
